title: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When no constraint such as engineering design or natural selection forces simple behavior, the rules that operate in nature are effectively selected in no special way apart from tending to be structurally simple, so they behave like randomly chosen rules and are almost always universal when their behavior is not obviously simple.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: most rules that appear in nature can be viewed as being selected in no special way—save perhaps for the fact that the structure of the rules themselves tends to be fairly simple.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “The Content of the Principle” (from p. 719), p. 723. Scope: rules governing natural systems not constrained by engineering or natural selection

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.21

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Selected physical and biological model collections could test a narrow version. Existing data cannot establish that most unconstrained natural rules are effectively random or almost always universal.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Choose natural domains with inferred mechanistic rules, quantify rule-description complexity and evidence of selection constraints, and compare their distribution with a prespecified random-rule ensemble. Then test computational universality for the matched models where possible.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Inferred rules depend on model choice and observational scale.

Random selection requires an arbitrary measure over rule descriptions.

Nature supplies no unbiased sampling frame of governing rules.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Random simple programs are easy to sample, and some natural patterns have published generative models, so a weak comparison is possible on a few systems. Selected in no special way is not directly observed, and most of the comparison confounds the true mechanism with the analyst's choice of model. The data that exist cover a biased handful of visually striking systems rather than rules in nature at large.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For natural systems not designed and not under an identified selective constraint, extract a rule at an agreed level and compare it with a random sample of structurally simple rules. The claim is supported if those natural rules fall in the same behavioral classes as the random sample, and weakened if they cluster in a special non-universal subclass once the known constraints are removed.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The rule of a natural system is model-dependent, and a fitted cellular automaton is not the system's rule.

Observation favors patterns we notice, which can imitate selection even when the underlying rule was not selected.
